titleStmt.title: Where the Metaphor Breaks: A Review of Theses on the Metaphors of Digital-Textual History

dhq:authorInfo.dhq:affiliation: Beijing Normal University–École Normale Supérieure de Paris

dhq:bio.p: Ling Zi holds a PhD in Literary Theory from Beijing Normal University, with doctoral research conducted jointly at the École Normale Supérieure (Paris). Her research works at the intersection of poetics and the philosophy of science and technology, with a particular focus on the digital humanities.

dhq:abstract.p: This review assesses Martin Paul Eve’s Theses on the Metaphors of Digital-Textual History (2024), a study that treats the metaphors of digital writing, such as page, whitespace, window, and library, as historical artifacts to be excavated and read. Organized as seven “theses”, the book argues that each such metaphor passes from description, through rupture, to a prescriptive afterlife that constrains how we imagine text. This review distinguishes two registers in Eve’s approach: an archaeological one that recovers material histories, most strikingly that of the PDF, and an interpretive one that reads the politics of computational metaphor, most inventively in its account of software as a “reader”. Setting the book against earlier work on new-media metaphor, it finds the archaeological chapters more persuasive, since their claims rest on archival evidence rather than analogy, and argues that the book’s methodological range exacts a cost in coherence. It concludes that the work is best read as a set of provocations rather than as a system.

dhq:teaser.p: A book review of Martin Paul Eve's Theses on the Metaphors of Digital-Textual History

body.p: Aim and Context

Martin Paul Eve opens Theses on the Metaphors of Digital-Textual History [Eve 2024a] with two fables of totality: Borges’s Library of Babel, which holds every book that could ever be written [Borges 1998, 112–18] [Eve 2024a, 1–2], and Langdale’s satirical πfs filesystem, which stores nothing and instead computes each file, on demand, from the digits of π [Eve 2024a, 3]. Eve reads both as illustrations of his point of departure: in the computational era, text and number are indistinguishable, since “any computer file ... can be expressed as a number” [Eve 2024a, pp. 2-4]. To write a history of text today is thus to write a history of computers and of numbers [Eve 2024a, 4]. It is this entanglement that the book pursues across seven “theses”: each interrogating a borrowed metaphor (page, whitespace, window, library) through which we make sense of born-digital text (text composed in digital form rather than digitized from print), and each tracing how that metaphor first describes, then breaks, and finally constrains what we can imagine.

Eve has written extensively on open access and scholarly communication, and the book, fittingly, is a study of how digital text circulates that itself circulates freely: it is issued under a Creative Commons license in Stanford University Press’s Text Technologies series. It is, in his words, the product of “a decade of thinking about critical approaches to text technology” [Eve 2024a, 5]. Nearly all text is now born-digital, and Eve extends the lineage of book history from Darnton’s “what is the history of books?” [Darnton 1982] toward its digital-material successor [Eve 2024a, 4]. His method is twofold. As a forensic reader of specific technologies, he follows Kirschenbaum [Kirschenbaum 2008] and shares Montfort’s wariness of “screen essentialism”, the assumption that the screen is where digital text really lives [Montfort 2004] [Eve 2024a, 17–18]. But he also practices Steven Connor’s “cultural phenomenology”, which attends to habits, substances, and textures of experience rather than to abstract structures, in a less forensic, more associative key [Connor 1999] [Eve 2024a, 19–21]. What is genuinely new is the object: Eve writes, for the first time, “about textuality without reading a set of texts,” turning instead to the “para-apparatuses,” the metadata, environments, and metaphors that frame digital text rather than constituting its content [Eve 2024a, 6–7]. The attention to computational metaphor is not itself new. It is the explicit subject of Marianne van den Boomen’s Transcoding the Digital [van den Boomen 2014], which Eve acknowledges as a precursor, and it anchors Wendy Chun’s influential account of software as “a metaphor for metaphor”, the universal machine that serves as both instrument and symptom of contemporary power [Chun 2011]. Eve turns in the opposite direction from Chun: where she reads the metaphor as it operates now, he excavates the long material pasts from which each metaphor was carried over. That historical depth is the book’s signal contribution; it is also, as the later chapters reveal, what most tests the coherence of the whole.
Methodology, Structure, and Content

The seven theses fall into two registers. The first is archaeological, recovering the material histories of specific technologies: whitespace, pagination, and digital preservation. The second is interpretive, reading the politics encoded in computational metaphors: those of Unicode, browsers, windows, and code libraries. The division is not merely expository; it reflects a career divided between hands-on infrastructure and cultural criticism. As a developer at Crossref, Eve has measured the very fragility he theorizes here, finding that some 28% of DOI-registered articles appear entirely unpreserved [Eve 2024b], and has anatomized the pirate “shadow library” as a minimal-maximal computational form [Eve 2022]. Theses is where that empirical work condenses into cultural theory.

The archaeological register is where the book is most persuasive, in large part because its claims rest on archival evidence rather than on analogy. Drawing on fresh correspondence with the format’s creators, Eve reconstructs the unlikely history of the PDF, a format so slow in its early PostScript form that Steve Jobs did not want to demonstrate it on stage, and one the Adobe board urged John Warnock to abandon altogether [Eve 2024a, 42–43]. “The most widely used computer file format for document dissemination nearly never existed” [Eve 2024a, 43]: contingency, not inevitability, made the digital page. The same impulse animates the chapter on whitespace, which Eve traces not to the blankness of paper but to the seriality of the player piano and the punched card, so that the empty space of the screen acquires a mechanical, musical prehistory [Eve 2024a, 96–98]. If Kirschenbaum brought forensic attention to the hard drive and the word processor, Eve extends that method to the file format and the encoding standard, the strata of text that are usually treated as given.

The interpretive register is where the book is most inventive, though also where its claims lean hardest on analogy. Eve recasts the software that parses a file format, from Word documents to web pages, as a “reader” with its own competence [Eve 2024a, 146–49]. A dominant but non-compliant browser such as Internet Explorer could thus make its own misreadings authoritative, so that “bad, antistandardized readings become de facto correct readings” and authors, in turn, learn to write badly [Eve 2024a, 151]. The political charge of these metaphors is clearest in the chapter on Unicode, where Eve shows that the apparently neutral work of character encoding is geopolitically conditioned. The Japanese kokuji taito, the most graphically complex character in the Han system at eighty-four strokes, entered the standard only in 2020; the characters that would most benefit from digitization, Eve observes, “are not digitized, because they are not frequently used, because they are difficult to write by hand” [Eve 2024a, 111–12]. The chapter on windows makes the same point through disability: inclusive design, caught in an “oscillating dialectic between the specific and the abstract,” obliges the designer “to sacrifice individualism in the service of communal catering for difference” of body and ability [Eve 2024a, 205]. The chapter on code libraries completes the argument, reading Stack Overflow as “the synecdochical library of the future,” a store of recombinable fragments governed less by altruism than by an economy of reputation and anxiety [Eve 2024a, 249].

The two registers seldom converse. Individual chapters can also wander: the preservation chapter moves from legal deposit to smallpox to gain-of-function research before returning to digital archives [Eve 2024a, 253, 277–80]. Both tendencies prompt the question Eve himself poses, whether the theses “add up to a coherent whole” [Eve 2024a, 24].
Conclusion

At its best, Theses on the Metaphors of Digital-Textual History shows how to read digital text through its metaphors. The recovered history of the PDF and the account of the browser as an interpreter of standards together dismantle any sense that the digital page, or the formats we now take for granted, were ever inevitable. In that telling, the book speaks directly to current concerns in the digital humanities: Eve’s dissection of Unicode extends debates on digital colonialism and multilingual text standards, while his reading of code libraries and preservation bears on the emerging field of critical infrastructure studies. Two reservations temper the achievement. The first is coherence, a consequence of method: since Connor’s cultural phenomenology proceeds by “a series of inveiglings” rather than by system [Eve 2024a, 20], it leaves the reader with seven sharp theses but no eighth to bind them into a portable argument, and makes the tightly argued chapters on pagination and browsers more convincing than the diffuse chapter on preservation. The second concerns use. Eve openly grants that his findings, like W. W. Greg’s textual discoveries, may have “practically none” of the bearing we might expect on how people actually write [Eve 2024a, 23]; he counters that they instead locate moments of “historical rupture and epistemic break” [Eve 2024a, 23]. Those seeking method will find it elsewhere in Eve’s work, in the concrete recommendations of his empirical studies [Eve 2024b]; this book offers provocation instead. Yet that is what the title promises: theses that loosen our inherited metaphors rather than build a system in their place. For the digital humanist, librarian, or book historian willing to follow its swerves, the reward is real: a sustained demonstration of how thin the metaphorical ground beneath our text technologies has always been [Eve 2024a, 296].
